title: The Possum

jokes.text: Tom gives Ann a teddy bear as a 'belated Valentine's Day' gift a full month after Valentine's Day, then immediately pivots to 'Happy early Valentine's Day' when called out
jokes.setup: Tom presents a gift to Ann as a 'Happy belated Valentine's Day' gesture
jokes.punchline: Ann points out Valentine's Day was a month ago; Tom immediately reframes it as 'Happy early Valentine's Day' for next year with zero shame
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom Haverford shamelessness — he never admits defeat, just reframes his failure as a new plan. The pivot from 'belated' to 'early' is quick and perfectly in character. Good structure but not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You're giving me a Valentine's Day gift in March?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's not late, it's an early gift for next year.

jokes.text: Tom insists the teddy bear is 'a regular, camera-less teddy bear' then immediately says 'Just put it in your bedroom, don't even think about it. It's a robot bear. It's programmed to snuggle!'
jokes.setup: Ann correctly suspects the bear is a nanny-cam; Tom denies it
jokes.punchline: Tom's denial immediately collapses as he reveals it IS robotic and instructs Ann to put it specifically in her bedroom
jokes.explanation: 'It's programmed to snuggle!' is a great absurdist escalation that makes the denial funnier in retrospect. The rapid self-contradiction and the specific instruction to put it in the bedroom compounds the creepiness comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's a camera.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No it's not. It's a camera-less bear. They're very popular in bear culture right now.

jokes.text: Donna takes the bear after hearing it has a camera in it, saying simply 'I know.'
jokes.setup: Ann warns Donna the bear has a camera inside it
jokes.punchline: Donna takes it anyway and says 'I know' — she wants to be filmed, or wants the camera for her own purposes
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum comic payload. Donna's 'I know' perfectly subverts the warning — she's not alarmed, she's delighted. Completely character-specific: Donna's unabashed confidence in her own desirability makes this land. Economy is nearly perfect. A small gem.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Come on, Ann, just put the bear in the nursery. It's a nanny cam.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, that's insane. I'm not putting a hidden camera in my baby's room.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's not hidden, it's just a bear. A regular bear that watches things.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's literally a hidden camera.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, what if I told you it's not a nanny cam? It's a robot bear that was programmed to snuggle with infants. Very expensive. Very rare. Comes from Sweden.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The snuggling is just a bonus feature of the surveillance—I mean, companionship software.

jokes.text: Ann's talking-head: 'I'm paying April 50 bucks to watch my house while I'm away. I would have asked Leslie, but I've seen the way she takes care of her house.'
jokes.setup: Ann explains why she chose April over her best friend Leslie to house-sit
jokes.punchline: The implication that Leslie is somehow a worse choice than the openly hostile April — because of how Leslie keeps her own house
jokes.explanation: Functional character joke implying Leslie is chaotically messy, which fits her hyperactive personality. Mild laugh — the joke is mostly in the implication and relies on audience knowledge of Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: There's a hidden camera in here.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Ann's talking-head ends with 'Maybe even... I don't like Ann. Become friends. Who knows?' — intercut with April's simultaneous confessional 'I don't like Ann.'
jokes.setup: Ann sweetly narrates her hope that house-sitting will bring her and April closer, maybe even to friendship
jokes.punchline: Cut to April flatly stating 'I don't like Ann' mid-sentence, then cut back to Ann finishing '…Become friends. Who knows?'
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in mockumentary editing as comedy. The intercutting of April's blunt 'I don't like Ann' directly into Ann's hopeful monologue is structurally elegant — the show's format becomes the punchline delivery mechanism. April's deadpan specificity and Ann's oblivious optimism are both perfectly in character. This is mockumentary craft at its best.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine, I won't read your mail.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'll just steam it open.

jokes.text: Leslie greets the mayor's aide: 'Oh, hello! I've always dreamed of you.' Then immediately corrects: 'Excuse me? Meeting you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is introduced to an important representative from the mayor's office and begins a formal greeting
jokes.punchline: Leslie accidentally says she's 'always dreamed of' the stranger — a Freudian slip revealing her desperate ambition — then poorly self-corrects
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie Knope overeagerness made manifest as a verbal slip. Her ambition is so consuming she accidentally reveals it to a stranger from the mayor's office. The beat-beat correction lands well. Solidly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Don't give Tom your keys. He'll just make copies of them.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know.

jokes.text: Leslie's elaborate taxonomy of the Parks Department's Most Wanted Pest List, including 'Poopy the raccoon who poops all over the high school cafeteria'
jokes.setup: The mayor's aide mentions a possum bit the mayor's dog; Leslie already knows about it
jokes.punchline: Leslie rattles off a bureaucratic 'Most Wanted Pest List' complete with animal nicknames and scatological detail, delivered with total earnestness
jokes.explanation: The joke is Leslie's total commitment to an absurdly detailed internal ranking system for vermin. 'Poopy the raccoon' as an official designation — delivered bureaucratically — is perfectly Leslie. The layering of bats-pooping-on-bells, then Poopy-pooping-in-cafeteria, then Fairway Frank shows comic escalation. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I didn't ask Leslie to house-sit because she's a slob. Last time she stayed at my place, she left empty Thai takeout containers everywhere, used my good towels to clean up spilled wine, and somehow got dirt on my ceiling. I'm still not sure how that happened.

jokes.text: Leslie dismisses Animal Control: 'Let's be honest. Animal Control is not the most effective branch of our government. They're a bunch of burned-out morons.'
jokes.setup: Evelyn suggests Animal Control should handle the possum
jokes.punchline: Leslie, a government employee herself, viciously disparages a fellow government department with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Solid ironic joke — Leslie loves government but has zero problem torching a fellow department. The hypocrisy is funny. 'Burned-out morons' is a slightly lazy insult but her delivery in character saves it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't like Ann.

jokes.text: 'Ma'am, the next time we speak, we shall be dancing on the grave of a possum.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is assigned to catch the possum and assures the mayor's aide
jokes.punchline: Leslie's overblown, quasi-military declaration about catching a single possum — the grandiosity wildly mismatches the stakes
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. The pomposity and formal register ('we shall be dancing on the grave of a possum') applied to pest control is a perfect encapsulation of Leslie's character — epic seriousness about mundane tasks. Highly quotable, strong economy, uniquely Leslie. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have to say, I've always dreamed of you.

dialogue.speaker: Evelyn
dialogue.line: ...What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, I've dreamed of meeting you! Of meeting you. That came out wrong.

jokes.text: And hot orange juice, weirdly delicious.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just qualified coffee as only her favorite behind tea
jokes.punchline: She continues to add to the exceptions list with the absurd addition of hot orange juice — 'weirdly delicious'
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of hot drinks keeps building the joke past where you expect it to end. 'Hot orange juice, weirdly delicious' is a real absurdist beat — the 'weirdly' acknowledges she knows it's odd but she likes it anyway. Small but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Parks Department has an official 'Most Wanted Pest List' with rankings.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head explaining 'shoeshine head' — when you shine too many shoes and 'the fumes create a thunderstorm in your brain'
jokes.setup: Andy recently diagnosed himself with a condition he calls 'shoeshine head'
jokes.punchline: His medical explanation — fumes causing a 'thunderstorm in your brain' — is delivered with total earnest conviction
jokes.explanation: Andy Dwyer's self-diagnosis of a fictional ailment is pure character comedy. 'Thunderstorm in your brain' is a vivid, specific, medically nonsensical image delivered with complete sincerity. The self-diagnosis framing — 'Andy recently diagnosed himself' — is the perfect mockumentary setup. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The raccoon is literally named 'Poopy' and specializes in cafeteria defecation.

jokes.text: Cures for 'shoeshine head' include coffee, cheeseburgers, and napping on the floor
jokes.setup: Andy has established the fake medical condition of shoeshine head
jokes.punchline: The prescribed cures escalate from slightly plausible (coffee) to absurd (napping on the floor, specifically) — no bed, just floor
jokes.explanation: 'Napping on the floor' as a specific prescription is the escalating absurdist beat. The floor detail matters — not napping on a couch or bed, but specifically the floor, which says something about Andy's living situation and general lifestyle. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Animal Control? Have you seen Animal Control? They couldn't control a golden retriever at a petting zoo. That's not a government agency, that's a joke with a budget.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head reaction after being asked if he has code violations — long pause, then simply: 'Nope.'
jokes.setup: Mark asks Ron if he has any code violations, implying it would be fine if not
jokes.punchline: Cut to Ron's deadpan confessional — clearly an extended pause — delivering a flat 'Nope' that the audience knows is a lie
jokes.explanation: The mockumentary talking-head format makes one word — 'Nope' — deliver an enormous amount of comedy. We already know he's lying. The pause before it (inferred from the timestamp gap 04:02-04:06) is the real joke. Maximum economy, strong character integration. Nick Offerman's deadpan is perfectly served by this format.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I will catch that possum. And when I do, I'm going to dance on its grave. I'm going to dance so hard on that possum's grave that the ground will cave in and I'll fall into the possum's coffin and I'll have to fight my way out.

jokes.text: Leslie to Animal Control supervisor: 'We're acting under direct orders from Mayor Gunderson's dog.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to commandeer Animal Control resources for her task force
jokes.punchline: She frames the political authority as coming from the mayor's dog, Rufus — technically accurate but absurd
jokes.explanation: The logic is technically correct — the dog got bitten, triggering the whole mission — but framing it as 'orders from the mayor's dog' is delightfully absurd. Leslie's bureaucratic precision accidentally creates the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Welcome to Parks and Recreation. The exit is that way.

jokes.text: Animal Control supervisor says his two best guys are Harris and Brett, but they're not there — then immediately: 'Isn't that them, there?' 'Nope.' — and we see it clearly is them.
jokes.setup: Supervisor says his best guys aren't present
jokes.punchline: They are visibly, obviously right there — the supervisor's denial is transparent and shameless
jokes.explanation: Classic visual comedy — the blatant lie and the deadpan 'Nope' is a quick, effective gag. Sets up the incompetence of Animal Control that Leslie already predicted.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Is that a badge? Did you become a cop?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, Andy. It's a coffee maker. I'm bringing you coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh. That makes way more sense.

jokes.text: Eugene's Animal Control team can't start until Monday even though it's Wednesday.
jokes.setup: Leslie assigns Eugene and his team to the important task force.
jokes.punchline: 'We'll get to it first thing Monday.' 'Today's Wednesday.' — confirming Leslie's earlier claim that Animal Control is full of 'burned-out morons.'
jokes.explanation: A callback that pays off Leslie's burn on Animal Control. The fact that they literally can't start for five days on a Wednesday is perfect bureaucratic satire. Efficient and earned.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I always bring coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I have a ranking system. Coffee's number three. Hot chocolate is number two. And hot orange juice is number one.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not a thing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: Animal Control guys Brett and Harris hear about the possum on the golf course and casually ask if Leslie will just catch it herself and call them to pick it up — as if that's a reasonable work arrangement
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been assigned Animal Control's best officers for her task force
jokes.punchline: The 'best officers' immediately propose that Leslie do all the work while they just come pick up afterwards
jokes.explanation: Pays off Leslie's prediction that Animal Control are 'burned-out morons.' The complete absence of work ethic presented matter-of-factly is funny. Good callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have a condition called shoeshine head. It's very serious. The doctors say if I don't get coffee, my head starts to shine like a freshly polished shoe.

jokes.text: Andy immediately tackles the possum before any plan is executed, yelling 'I got it!' as Leslie is mid-sentence laying out the strategy
jokes.setup: Leslie carefully begins laying out a strategic flanking plan for catching the possum
jokes.punchline: Andy doesn't wait — he charges in and tackles it before the plan is even finished, operating purely on instinct
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural subversion — the elaborate setup/plan format is demolished by Andy acting before it can conclude. This is sitcom plotting serving the joke: Leslie's careful preparation vs. Andy's zero-planning instinct. The physical nature of it (he actually tackles a possum) amplifies the impact.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have a condition called Hibernation Syndrome. It's very rare. Basically, my body thinks it's a bear, so during the winter months, I need to consume massive quantities of food and then just sort of... shut down for a few months.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The doctors say it's caused by brain thunderstorms. That's when your brain gets all stormy and confused, like actual thunderstorms, but in your brain.

jokes.text: Animal Control officers lure Andy into their golf ball trap: 'Hey, want your ball back? Come with me.'
jokes.setup: Harris and Brett need to get Andy to join the task force without effort.
jokes.punchline: They lure him with a lost golf ball — and Andy, childlike, immediately follows them. 'Oh, man!'
jokes.explanation: A decent visual gag — the Animal Control guys using basic bait to catch Andy rather than the possum is funny in its implication. Andy's 'Oh, man!' suggests he's delighted to follow. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Treatment is just things Andy likes

jokes.text: The possum ends up on Andy's neck after he catches it; 'It's on my neck! Okay, okay, okay, okay! He's on my neck!'
jokes.setup: Andy triumphantly catches the possum
jokes.punchline: Victory immediately turns to panic as the possum attaches itself to Andy's neck
jokes.explanation: The consequence of Andy's reckless heroism arrives immediately. The repetition of 'okay, okay, okay' while reassuring people it's fine while a possum is on his neck is classic Andy chaos. Physical escalation works well here.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me that floor napping is a legitimate medical treatment?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: According to this pamphlet from 1987, yes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Finally! A cure for shoeshine head that doesn't involve a doctor!

jokes.text: 'Task force coming through! Task force clear. Resume golfing.'
jokes.setup: Leslie's task force marches through the golf course.
jokes.punchline: Leslie announces their presence and clearance with the authority of a SWAT commander — for a possum hunt on a public golf course.
jokes.explanation: 'Resume golfing' is the perfect kicker — the civilian dismissal after the tactical clearance. Economy is high, Leslie's militaristic overconfidence is perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Do you have any code violations?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Tiger Woods joke: 'I used to love Tiger Woods because he was a great champion. But after that sex scandal? The man is a god!'
jokes.setup: Tom apparently offers an unprompted opinion on Tiger Woods on the golf course
jokes.punchline: Tom's admiration for Tiger increases because of the sex scandal — the inverse of the expected moral judgment
jokes.explanation: The inversion is the joke — admiring Tiger more for the scandal is Tom. Topical at time of airing (2010). The joke is structurally simple and relies on the cultural moment. Solid but not timeless.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They said they'd handle the possum on Monday.

dialogue.speaker: Eugene
dialogue.line: It's Wednesday.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Ron's woodshop: no drainage, no ventilation, hazardous chemicals — Ron's defense: 'Yeah, which only I'm breathing. It's the same liberty that gives me the right to fart in my own car.'
jokes.setup: Mark catalogs the code violations in Ron's woodshop
jokes.punchline: Ron's libertarian defense of breathing hazardous chemicals alone equates it to the right to fart in your own car — a philosophically absurd but internally consistent argument
jokes.explanation: Ron's car-fart liberty argument is perfectly in character — it's not random absurdism, it's a coherent libertarian philosophy applied to hazardous chemical exposure. The analogy is genuinely funny AND reveals Ron's worldview. 'Are you gonna tell a man that he can't fart in his own car?' as a rhetorical stand-in for poisonous fumes is inspired.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? My authority comes directly from the mayor. And you know whose authority comes from me? The mayor's dog.

jokes.text: Mark finds a fire extinguisher that should have been recharged in June 1996. Ron: 'Those dates are arbitrary. They're like those expiration dates the government forces companies to put on yogurt and medicine.'
jokes.setup: Mark points out the fire extinguisher is dangerously out of date
jokes.punchline: Ron dismisses safety expiration dates with a libertarian philosophical argument that also applies to medicine expiration dates — potentially lethal position delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: The casual equation of fire extinguisher recertification with yogurt expiration dates is classic Ron: a consistent philosophy that sounds reasonable until you realize he's also dismissing medicine expiration dates in a room full of hazardous chemicals. Dark undertone makes it funnier. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Eugene
dialogue.line: My best guys aren't here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But they're right there.

dialogue.speaker: Eugene
dialogue.line: No, they're not.

jokes.text: After the extinguisher demonstration, Ron says flatly: 'Okay. I'll replace this. Happy?'
jokes.setup: Ron just defended the extinguisher as perfectly fine
jokes.punchline: The immediate concession — 'Okay. I'll replace this. Happy?' — suggests the demonstration did NOT go well, Ron knows it, and he's moving on without acknowledging it
jokes.explanation: The complete about-face after his confident 'Observe' is the payoff. Ron's dignity is intact in his delivery — he doesn't explain, he just concedes and moves on. Perfect economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Here, Brett, I got you something. A golf ball!

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Oh wow, thanks Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're welcome, homie.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Wait, my name is Brett, not Homie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, I was just being friendly.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Oh. I thought you were calling me by my actual name that I didn't know about.

jokes.text: Tom on the golf course: 'How long do you think it would take me to learn golf, Leslie?' / 'I could teach you... you have to get up early, hit the range, practice reading greens.' / 'Yeah, I don't want to do all that. I think I just want some of those dope pants.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks Leslie how long it would take to learn golf, implying interest
jokes.punchline: He immediately rejects all the work involved — he only wants the aesthetic (the 'dope pants') without any of the substance
jokes.explanation: Very Tom Haverford — all style, no substance. The pivot from 'how do I learn golf' to 'I just want the pants' is fast and perfectly in character. 'Dope pants' as the specific golf aspiration is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have to say, I'm really disappointed in Tiger Woods. I've always admired him, but what he did was just... morally reprehensible.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, no, that's not true. After I found out about all those affairs, my respect for him went way up. That man is a champion.

jokes.text: Mark counts 28 violations in rapid succession in Ron's woodshop.
jokes.setup: Mark is cataloguing the violations in Ron's shop while Ron is distracted by the possum chaos.
jokes.punchline: He reaches 28 violations, which implies the shop is almost entirely in violation — a visual escalation of the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A background joke — Mark silently counting while chaos erupts around him. The sheer number (28) is funny. Not a top-tier joke but works well as a running background beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Welcome to my workshop. You're the first non-me to ever set foot in here.

jokes.text: Leslie gives the flanking plan to the Animal Control officers and Andy — then Andy immediately charges before she finishes
jokes.setup: Leslie carefully outlines positions: 'You two, flank the left. I'll flank the right. Andy will come in to—'
jokes.punchline: Andy charges before Leslie can finish assigning his role
jokes.explanation: The interrupted sentence IS the punchline — we never learn what role Leslie had in mind for Andy because he's already gone. Perfect structural efficiency. The cut-off is the joke, which is great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: The workshop isn't up to code.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It meets my personal 'Swanson Code.'

jokes.text: After the capture: 'I was just the simple mastermind who planned the whole operation and executed it to perfection.' The reporter immediately redirects to Andy.
jokes.setup: Leslie takes credit for the operation going smoothly
jokes.punchline: The reporter immediately redirects to Andy, the person who actually caught it — undercutting Leslie's self-aggrandizement
jokes.explanation: 'Simple mastermind' is a great oxymoron that Leslie uses unironically. The immediate redirect by Evelyn perfectly punctures Leslie's self-importance. Good economy and character work.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have the right to ignore safety codes in my own establishment, just like I have the fundamental right to fart in my own car.

jokes.text: 'You're next, Poopy.' — Andy's threat to the raccoon, after catching the possum
jokes.setup: Andy has just caught the possum on his neck; the Parks Most Wanted Pest List was established earlier
jokes.punchline: Andy, with a possum on his neck, issues a direct threat to Poopy the raccoon — still addressing the possum situation, already moving on to the next target
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous comedy payload. The callback to Poopy (established earlier as #2 on the Most Wanted Pest List) is perfectly timed. Andy — with a possum still on his neck — already thinking about the next mission is so on-brand it's almost beautiful. The specificity of Poopy as the addressee makes this a great callback. Economy is near perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Ron, this fire extinguisher expired in 1998.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Expiration dates are just a government conspiracy to make you buy more things. This extinguisher is fine.

jokes.text: 'Please, my friends call me Andy Radical.' — 'No, we don't.'
jokes.setup: The reporter is introduced to Andy Dwyer as the possum hero
jokes.punchline: Andy insists his nickname is 'Andy Radical'; Leslie immediately denies this nickname exists
jokes.explanation: A perfectly compact two-beat joke. Andy's unsolicited self-branding ('Andy Radical') is immediately demolished by Leslie's flat 'No, we don't.' The deadpan negation is funnier than any elaboration would be. Highly quotable and a perfect encapsulation of Andy's delusion vs. reality.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, I appreciate the offer, but I gotta be honest with you. I'm not really interested in golf.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Why not? It's a great sport!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because I don't care about hitting a ball around a field. What I care about is the outfits. The visors, the pastel polos, the little argyle socks. That's the dream.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So you want to learn golf just for the clothes?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, I want to BE golf fashion. That's the real game.

jokes.text: Andy's self-introduction: 'By day, Andy Dwyer, shoeshine-ist. By a different time of day, Andy Radical, possum tackler. And by night, I do whatever I want. No job.'
jokes.setup: Andy introduces himself to the reporter in heroic terms
jokes.punchline: The tripartite 'by day/by night' structure collapses: 'by a different time of day' replaces the expected 'by night'; the actual night reveal is 'I do whatever I want. No job.'
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The classic superhero 'by day X, by night Y' structure is subverted at every beat: (1) 'by a different time of day' is a perfect comic substitution for 'by night,' (2) 'Andy Radical, possum tackler' as the heroic alter-ego is absurd, (3) the night reveal — 'I do whatever I want. No job.' — is pure pathos played as comedy. The period after 'whatever I want' followed by 'No job' as its own sentence is brilliant structure. This is character comedy at its finest — it tells you everything about Andy in three sentences. Comparable to the calibration anchors in terms of quotability and structural elegance. Justifies the 9.0.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, we need to move very slowly around the possum. Nice and easy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Nope!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm out!

jokes.text: Leslie immediately starts listing 'special favors' she wants from the mayor's office: extra recycling can, laminated bus pass, 'What time do you usually go to sleep? Because my best ideas usually come to me at night.'
jokes.setup: Evelyn tells Leslie she can call for a special favor from the mayor any time
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately tries to exploit this for a series of increasingly mundane and then invasive requests, culminating in asking the aide's bedtime for late-night calls
jokes.explanation: Great escalation from mundane (recycling can) to inappropriate (what time do you sleep so I can call you). The bedtime question is the perfect overstep. Leslie's inability to pace herself or read a room is central to her character and comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'll make you a canoe.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Ron, that's not going to fix the code violations.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A canoe fixes everything.

jokes.text: Leslie's farewell to the mayor's aide: 'See you in hell, buddy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie wraps up her meeting with the mayor's aide on positive terms
jokes.punchline: She closes with the completely inappropriate 'See you in hell, buddy' as if it's a standard goodbye
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and weird in the best way. The total contextual inappropriateness of 'see you in hell' as a professional goodbye is the joke. Economy is near perfect. Very Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: OK, so here's the careful plan we need to follow...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: AHHHH! POSSUM!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: tackles the possum

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head on possum certainty: 'Am I sure the possum we caught is Fairway Frank? Yes. Am I quite sure? No. Am I sure enough? Maybe.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reflects on whether they caught the right possum
jokes.punchline: Her escalating qualifications (yes → no → maybe) undercut each other perfectly; the final 'Could I live with myself? That depends.' bottoms out into a non-answer
jokes.explanation: The structure of this talking-head is outstanding. Each rhetorical question is answered and immediately undermined by the next. 'Yes / No / Maybe' is a perfect comic descending scale. 'Could I live with myself? That depends.' is a great capper that reveals Leslie's moral ambivalence while maintaining her authoritative tone. The final 'Uh...' on 'Does doing so help me make decisions?' is the cherry on top — even her meta-process doesn't work. Strongly structured, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fairway Frank, you listen to me. I know you've been watching us. I know you've seen what we're capable of. So here's what's going to happen: you're going to leave this park, you're going to leave Pawnee, and you're never going to come back. Because if you do, I will find every single one of your raccoon friends, and I will make sure they know that you are no longer welcome in this town.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And Trash Panda? Yeah, I'm talking to you too. Stop eating our garbage. This is your only warning.

jokes.text: Andy introduces himself to reporter Shauna by referencing the article she wrote when he 'fell in the pit' — and then, matter-of-factly: 'And then afterwards, had sex with Mark and everyone talked about it.'
jokes.setup: Andy greets the reporter by referencing her previous coverage of him
jokes.punchline: He casually tacks on the detail about her having sex with Mark (another colleague) as if it's a neutral biographical fact, with no social awareness
jokes.explanation: Andy's total social obliviousness — casually recapping a professional contact's sex life to her face as if completing a bio — is peak Andy. The cringe discomfort is real but played with Andy's earnest sweetness making it funny rather than mean. The 'and everyone talked about it' adds the perfect detail.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You can call me 'The Neon Leopard.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Leslie interrupts the reporter's line of questioning about Fairway Frank to insist the possum be called 'just a possum' — setting up a correction that immediately undermines the whole mission
jokes.setup: The reporter starts asking questions about Fairway Frank specifically
jokes.punchline: Leslie, who built the whole mission on Fairway Frank's identity, now hedges and says to refer to it just as 'a possum' — revealing her own uncertainty
jokes.explanation: A nice ironic beat — the person who named the possum 'Fairway Frank' and led the task force to catch him now insists on generic language. Sets up the B-plot tension about possum identity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: By night, I'm a completely different person.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm unemployed.

jokes.text: Andy's interview logic: 'When you're in a situation, you don't have time to think. So I thought to myself, Don't think, Andy, act.' / 'So you weren't thinking?' / 'Not at all. I cannot emphasize enough how little I was thinking.'
jokes.setup: Reporter asks Andy how he acted so quickly to catch the possum
jokes.punchline: Andy's logic is self-defeating — he describes the process of thinking in order to explain he wasn't thinking — and then proudly doubles down: 'I cannot emphasize enough how little I was thinking.'
jokes.explanation: 'I cannot emphasize enough how little I was thinking' is a standout line. The structure is tight: the logical paradox of thinking about not thinking, the reporter's gentle catch ('so you weren't thinking?'), and Andy's enthusiastic confirmation that demolishes any heroic framing. Highly quotable, perfectly Andy. Justifies 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need you to call me at home. Late at night. With ideas.

dialogue.speaker: Evelyn
dialogue.line: Ma'am, it's almost midnight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. That's when the ideas come.

jokes.text: Andy describes his vermin friends from the pit: 'You know what? "Friends" sounds stupid. Colleagues. They are bad at sharing, but they are good at tag.'
jokes.setup: Andy describes bonding with animals while living in the pit
jokes.punchline: He self-corrects 'friends' to the more professional 'colleagues,' then characterizes these animal colleagues with specific, absurd, behavioral notes
jokes.explanation: The shift from 'friends' to 'colleagues' to describe pit rats is a perfect comic register shift. The behavioral assessment — 'bad at sharing, good at tag' — is absurdist gold. It implies Andy actually studied these animals enough to have opinions on their social skills. This is highly specific, character-integrated comedy that reveals Andy's entire situation (he lived in a pit) while being extremely funny. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm absolutely certain about this decision.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, fairly certain.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, reasonably sure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I think so?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Maybe?

jokes.text: Reporter asks what Andy's girlfriend (the nurse) thinks about his heroism; Andy reveals the breakup: 'I broke up with Ann. Shortly after she kicked me out and told me we wouldn't be together anymore.'
jokes.setup: Reporter congratulates Andy on his heroism and asks what his nurse girlfriend thinks
jokes.punchline: Andy reframes Ann dumping him as 'I broke up with Ann' — shortly after she kicked him out and ended the relationship. He initiated the breakup by being broken up with.
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy self-deception — he 'broke up with' Ann in the sense that he was broken up with. The timeline he gives completely contradicts his framing. The joke is in the specificity: 'shortly after she kicked me out and told me we wouldn't be together anymore.' Andy's earnest cognitive dissonance about his own life is perfectly rendered.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have a very specific decision-making process. First, I make a list of pros and cons. Then I sleep on it. Then I wake up and I think about it some more. Then I usually just do whatever I want anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Does that process work?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have no idea. I've never actually completed it.

jokes.text: Reporter suggests the article might win Ann back; Andy: 'What now?' — long pause — 'I hadn't even thought of that. Wow. Of all the things I thought would bring us back together, catching a possum was never on that list.'
jokes.setup: Reporter offhandedly suggests the heroic article might change Ann's mind
jokes.punchline: Andy's genuine shock and the implication that he has an actual list of things that might win Ann back — none of which were possum-related
jokes.explanation: The implication of an existing (non-possum) list of win-Ann-back strategies is a great piece of character world-building through comedy. 'What now?' as genuine shock at a simple observation is perfectly Andy. Warm and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, Shauna wrote this article about me being incompetent, which—whatever, fair point. But then she also wrote about how she was having an affair with Mark, which she didn't even tell me about!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I just casually mentioned it in front of everyone at the meeting. She was NOT happy.

jokes.text: Tom puts on golf clothes and declares: 'Seriously, man, when you wear these clothes, you just feel better than everyone else. You know?'
jokes.setup: Tom had earlier said he just wanted 'those dope pants.'
jokes.punchline: Now wearing the golf clothes, he's exactly as he predicted — feeling superior. The callback confirms Tom's entire personality.
jokes.explanation: A nice callback payoff. Tom was right — wearing the pants immediately makes him feel superior. His sincere 'You know?' addressed to someone who clearly doesn't know is Tom Haverford at his most Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't think before I act. That's my strength. I'm like a superhero, except instead of thinking, I just do stuff and hope it works out.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'I just want you to know that I still don't think city codes...' Mark: 'Ron, shut up.'
jokes.setup: Mark has taken a half-day to help Ron bring the woodshop up to code as a friend
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately starts philosophizing against city codes; Mark shuts him down before he can finish the sentence
jokes.explanation: Mark's pre-emptive 'Ron, shut up' is a great beat. He knows what's coming and refuses to hear it. The friendship dynamic makes the bluntness warm rather than hostile. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I work with pit vermin— I mean, colleagues.

jokes.text: Ron arrives in Leslie's office wearing a golf glove with a pom-pom that 'fell off' — he pretends to have come in to search for the pom-pom as a pretense for checking on Mark
jokes.setup: Ron needs an excuse to be in Leslie's office to check on something
jokes.punchline: Ron Swanson, the ultra-macho libertarian, wanders in wearing a golf glove with a decorative pom-pom, asking people to help him look for it on the floor
jokes.explanation: The visual of Ron in a golf glove with a pom-pom is the comedy. His elaborate transparent pretense — combined with the incongruous accessory — is funny. The joke is mostly physical/visual. Works better on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ben is like the organized spreadsheet guy. April is the one who makes everything weird and dark. Ron is basically a wood-working hermit who hates government. Leslie is... she's like if enthusiasm had a face and that face was running for office. Tom is just trying to hustle his way into being rich. Donna is the one person who actually has her life together and judges all of us for not having ours together.

jokes.text: Ron, discussing the pit project with Leslie: 'So, how's your hole?' Leslie answers seriously, then catches herself — 'Excuse me? The pit.'
jokes.setup: Ron asks about the progress on Leslie's park project — referring to the pit/Lot 48
jokes.punchline: Ron's question 'how's your hole?' is an innocent reference to the pit, but lands as a double entendre
jokes.explanation: A fairly standard double entendre that the show is aware of and plays straight. The joke is in the clarification 'Excuse me? The pit.' It's functional but not particularly inventive — accidental double entendres are common sitcom territory.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, so Ann broke up with me. But I got there first. I broke up with her, and then she broke up with me. So technically, I broke up with her first.

jokes.text: Leslie shows the reporter a business card and begins over-pitching it: 'This isn't a really big story, right? Nobody cares about this very much.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is excited about a potential front-page story about the possum
jokes.punchline: She attempts reverse psychology on the reporter by insisting the story isn't important — transparently doing the opposite
jokes.explanation: Leslie's reverse-psychology attempt is transparent and therefore funny, but it's a relatively common beat. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. This article could help me win Ann back! I'm gonna be famous!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'll finally have something to show her. A real accomplishment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh man, Ann's gonna see this and realize what she's been missing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I mean, possum-catching. That's gotta be relationship repair gold, right?

jokes.text: Tom's song about Fairway Frank: 'Fairway Frank, you're gonna die / You're gonna fry, oh yeah / You guilty son of a bitch / You're gonna fry, when they flip that switch'
jokes.setup: Tom is walking the golf course after the possum has been caught
jokes.punchline: Tom has composed and is performing a gleeful, profane death-penalty song about a possum, with full musical commitment
jokes.explanation: Tom singing a death-sentence song for a possum — 'when they flip that switch' — is gloriously unhinged. The profanity ('you guilty son of a bitch') against the target of a small woodland animal is the escalating absurdism. The musical commitment and lyrical specificity make this memorable. Tom's joy in it is the real joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I wear expensive clothes because they make me feel superior to other people. And that's what I'm gonna keep doing.

jokes.text: April's confessional about the possum identity crisis, told through an elaborate whale metaphor that she maintains until she breaks: 'I saw a second possum!'
jokes.setup: April is wrestling with telling someone there might be a second possum
jokes.punchline: She constructs an elaborate hypothetical whale/fish/submarine metaphor to avoid saying it directly, then abandons it entirely: 'I saw a second possum!'
jokes.explanation: The whale metaphor is a funny choice for April to use — it's her reluctance to be helpful made absurdly elaborate. The sudden abandonment of the metaphor ('I saw a second possum!') is the right punchline. Good character work showing April trying to maintain detachment while actually caring.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey everyone, I just bought a banana for $1.50 at this new organic market and I gotta tell you, it's really changed my life.

jokes.text: Tom's description of Andy kissing his own biceps during the photo shoot
jokes.setup: Tom is updating April on Andy's magazine interview situation
jokes.punchline: Andy is 'literally kissing his own biceps' during the heroic photo shoot — an act of delusional self-celebration
jokes.explanation: The visual of Andy kissing his own biceps is funny on its own, and fits his earnest self-aggrandizement perfectly. Economy is good — 'literally kissing his own biceps' does a lot of work in five words.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! Ron, did you see that article about the pom-pom shortage?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, there's a massive pom-pom shortage. I'm reading it right now on my phone.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, there's no pom-pom shortage.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh wow, look at that. The article just... disappeared. Must be a really big story.

jokes.text: Andy tells April about his photo shoot: 'I think I nailed it. I fell off the stool once when I was trying to look serious, but I'm okay.'
jokes.setup: Andy updates April on how his heroic photo shoot went
jokes.punchline: His confident assessment ('I nailed it') is immediately undermined by revealing he fell off the stool while trying to look serious — and the 'I'm okay' suggests it was a real fall
jokes.explanation: The structure is tight: confident declaration, immediate self-undermining detail, reassurance. The 'I'm okay' as a coda implies it was bad enough that it needed addressing. 'Trying to look serious' as the context for falling is perfect — it's trying so hard to be cool that it creates failure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: 🎵 Possum, possum, on the ground, you're the meanest thing around. Possum, possum, electric chair, we're gonna fry you fair and square. 🎵

jokes.text: April to Andy, on waiting for his photos: 'Yeah, that sounds good, but I can't because I have to go do something that actually matters.'
jokes.setup: Andy enthusiastically invites April to wait with him for the emailed photos
jokes.punchline: April declines with a burn — 'something that actually matters' — a devastating dismissal dressed as a neutral reason
jokes.explanation: Classic April — the dismissal is delivered with zero expression, which makes it land harder. The economy is excellent. The twist is that she's actually going to do something to help Andy (find the truth about the possum), making the subtext warmly ironic on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So, hypothetically, if there were these large, nocturnal creatures that ate garbage and hissed at people... how would one address that in a town hall meeting?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, why are you talking like that? Just say possum.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm being subtle. You see, these creatures are like whales. Majestic whales that swim through our trash cans at night, breaching—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: They're possums. They don't swim.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude! The ocean is just a metaphor for the streets, Ben. Why does everyone keep interrupting my whale presentation?

jokes.text: The golf course groundskeeper is shown photos and confirms it's Fairway Frank — but the photos shown are of three different possums. Groundskeeper: 'Huh.'
jokes.setup: April asks the groundskeeper to identify Fairway Frank from photos to confirm they caught the right possum
jokes.punchline: He confirms all three different-looking possums as Fairway Frank; when called out — 'those are three different possums' — he just says 'Huh.' No defense, no explanation
jokes.explanation: 'Huh.' as the response to discovering you've been confidently misidentifying multiple possums is a great deadpan. The complete absence of shame or explanation is perfectly funny. Also confirms Animal Control's incompetence and the entire possum-ID problem. One syllable does a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I'm not motivated by jealousy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Possums are adorable.

jokes.text: While April and Leslie try to figure out the possum situation, another possum is spotted on the 14th green — Animal Control immediately offered to come take it
jokes.setup: Animal Control has been established as incompetent morons who wouldn't do anything
jokes.punchline: They are immediately available and willing to take the OTHER possum, having done nothing about the original for presumably years
jokes.explanation: Good ironic callback — the 'useless' Animal Control instantly springs to action for a different possum. Suggests there are possums everywhere and they've been doing nothing about the right one. Functional payoff of the running Animal Control incompetence gag.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I totally nailed it. I fell off the stool like three times, but I kept getting back up and nailing it.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head can't list her shortcomings: 'I can't kill the possum because it might be innocent. I can't let it go because it might be guilty. I can't make a good soup, can't do a handstand in a pool, can't spell the word lieutenant. There's a lot of can'ts in my life right now.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is wrestling with the moral dilemma of the possibly-wrong possum
jokes.punchline: Her list of current limitations escalates from the moral/professional to the deeply personal and random (soup, handstand, lieutenant), revealing she's catastrophizing
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'possum guilt' to 'making soup' to 'handstand in a pool' to 'spelling lieutenant' is outstanding comedy writing. Each item gets more absurd and personal. The concluding 'There's a lot of can'ts in my life right now' is the perfect deflated capper. The specificity of 'lieutenant' — a genuinely difficult word — is the absurdist detail that makes it memorable. One of the episode's strongest jokes. Highly quotable and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, isn't this amazing? I'm so excited!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, right? You're so excited you can't even speak!

jokes.text: 'Let's make it happen, Captain.' / 'Don't call me that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie rallies April with a motivational send-off
jokes.punchline: April flatly refuses the nickname
jokes.explanation: Quick and clean. April's rejection of the affectionate nickname maintains her character's carefully cultivated indifference. Not a standout joke but well executed in its economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: That's Fairway Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Campopiano
dialogue.line: Huh.

jokes.text: Leslie's distraction: 'Help! Help, my arm looks like it's bleeding!' — and then immediately: 'Oh, look how much it's bleeding. Everybody look at it. I need everyone's full attention during this.'
jokes.setup: Leslie needs to distract Animal Control so April can sneak the possum out
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'distraction' is to fake-bleed, then over-direct the fake emergency with stage-management instructions: 'I need everyone's full attention during this'
jokes.explanation: The stage-management of her own fake emergency — 'I need everyone's full attention during this' — is perfectly Leslie. She can't do anything without turning it into a production. The ketchup reveal and Jerry's confirmation are good payoffs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, please, I need your help with the possum.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, come on. Please?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April! APRIL! Please help me with the possum!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would I do that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because you're my friend and I'm begging you on my knees for this possum!

jokes.text: Jerry's talking-head during the distraction scene: 'Sentry duty is usually approximately one hour long. Baby meerkats do not start foraging for food until about one month old. Do you know them?'
jokes.setup: Jerry is apparently tasked with being a lookout during Leslie's distraction
jokes.punchline: Jerry delivers a stream-of-consciousness talking-head that includes an irrelevant meerkat fact and then asks if the camera crew personally knows the meerkats
jokes.explanation: 'Do you know them?' — directed at the documentary crew about baby meerkats — is surreal and delightful. Jerry's non-sequitur meerkat facts followed by what seems like a genuine inquiry are absurdist and unique. Jerry's awkward, well-meaning uselessness is perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe I have to choose between saving an innocent possum and completing my park project. What kind of person does that make me? What kind of leader? What kind of friend?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, when I was six, I didn't finish my lemonade stand because I was worried about bees. My mother said I'd never accomplish anything. And she was right! Well, not about the lemonade stand—I actually did finish that. But about other things!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And Ben always knows exactly what to do in these situations. I bet he would have saved the possum AND finished the park by now. I'm a fraud. I'm a complete and utter fraud.

jokes.text: Leslie reveals where the possum is to Evelyn — in a house 'somewhere the mayor can never pee on it' — implying the mayor's plan is to pee on it
jokes.setup: Evelyn asks where the possum is being kept; Leslie proudly says it's somewhere the mayor can never 'pee on it'
jokes.punchline: Evelyn clarifies the mayor doesn't want to pee on it — he wants to taxidermy it and put it above the urinal so 'little flecks of pee can get on it forever'
jokes.explanation: The escalating bathroom-based revenge plan is wonderfully specific. Leslie's assumption that the mayor wants to pee ON the possum is corrected by an even more elaborate/gross alternative: taxidermied above a urinal for perpetual pee-flecking. 'Little flecks of pee can get on it forever' is a specific, indelible image. The escalation from gross to MORE gross works well. Justifies 8+ through specificity and absurdist commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh no! Oh no no no! I think I've twisted my ankle! Someone call a doctor!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The pain! The excruciating pain! I may never walk again!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is the worst day of my entire life. Somebody get me ice. And a wheelchair. And someone to fan me with a large leaf!

jokes.text: Evelyn reveals the mayor wants to 'stuff it and hang it above the urinal in his office bathroom so that little flecks of pee can get on it forever.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if the mayor wants to have sex with a dead possum (itself a joke — see below). Evelyn clarifies 'He's not a monster.'
jokes.punchline: The actual plan is to taxidermy it and mount it above his urinal specifically so it gets peed on forever. This is somehow worse than nothing, and 'He's not a monster' is now retroactively funny.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely original, dark, and unexpected joke. The setup of 'He's not a monster' followed by a plan that involves deliberately ensuring 'little flecks of pee can get on it forever' is a masterclass in subverted expectation. The specificity of 'little flecks' is grotesquely funny. The mayor is somehow more petty and disgusting than any sexual predator — he just wants to eternally urinate on his enemy. Exceptional dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, is this your blood?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I... I don't think so?

jokes.text: Evelyn clarifying: 'He's not a monster. He wants to stuff it and hang it above the urinal in his office bathroom so that little flecks of pee can get on it forever.'
jokes.setup: Leslie assumes the mayor wants to pee directly on the dead possum
jokes.punchline: Evelyn corrects this with a more elaborate — but still scatological — plan, delivered with professional seriousness
jokes.explanation: Part of the same joke sequence as #57 but strong enough to note separately. 'He's not a monster' followed by the taxidermy-urinal plan is the perfect deadpan. The professional delivery of a grotesque plan by a formal government aide is the character-based comedy. 'Little flecks of pee can get on it forever' deserves to be a famous line.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm standing guard over this possum. Did you know that meerkats can go their entire lives without drinking water? They get all their moisture from their food. Fascinating creatures. Unlike this possum, which is just disgusting.

jokes.text: Leslie refuses to reveal the possum's location 'no matter how much you ask me,' then immediately says she'll stop talking 'because I'm afraid I may accidentally say where it is.'
jokes.setup: Leslie heroically declares she won't reveal the possum's location.
jokes.punchline: She immediately undercuts her own resolve by admitting she'll accidentally say it if she keeps talking — and then rushes Evelyn out.
jokes.explanation: A self-aware moment where Leslie's heroic resolve crumbles instantly — she knows herself well enough to know she'll spill it by accident. The meta-awareness of her own weakness is characterful and the structure is clean: heroic declaration immediately followed by honest self-assessment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What does the mayor want to do with the possum?

dialogue.speaker: Evelyn
dialogue.line: I... I don't know, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because I have some ideas, and they're not good.

dialogue.speaker: Evelyn
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

jokes.text: Tom reads about the 'innocent duck / vicious goose' case from Walnut Creek — Leslie's reaction: 'No, it's awful, Tom. How would you feel if you killed an innocent duck and let a vicious goose waddle free?'
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie are researching precedents for killing the wrong animal
jokes.punchline: Leslie's passionate moral framing of a duck-vs-goose misidentification — 'a vicious goose waddle free' — treats the case with full tragic weight
jokes.explanation: The Walnut Creek duck/goose case is a perfect absurdist parallel that Leslie uses as a genuine moral touchstone. 'A vicious goose waddle free' is a great phrase — the absurdity of 'waddle free' applied to criminal justice is funny. Sets up the possum identity moral dilemma with a ridiculous mirror.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The mayor wants a statue of himself in the center of town.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A statue? That's actually not the worst idea. We could make it really beautiful, really inspiring.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, Leslie. He wants it positioned over a public urinal so that for all of eternity, people will be urinating on his statue.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's grotesque.

jokes.text: Tom gets a call from April saying the possum escaped at Ann's house. He immediately promises April not to tell Leslie — and then the VERY next line: 'The possum got loose at Ann's house.'
jokes.setup: April calls Tom in panic about the escaped possum and explicitly says 'Don't tell Leslie'
jokes.punchline: Tom hangs up and immediately tells Leslie
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the instant betrayal — Tom says 'You got it' to April's 'Don't tell Leslie' and then the next line of dialogue is Tom telling Leslie. The gap between promise and betrayal is zero seconds. This is perfect structural sitcom timing. It's not a surprising joke (Tom would obviously tell Leslie) but the instantaneous nature of the betrayal is the comedy. Strong economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I won't reveal the possum's location.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Although, knowing me, I might accidentally reveal it while telling someone about how I won't reveal it.

jokes.text: April explains how the possum escaped: 'I let it out of its cage because it needed water, and I thought it would just drink out of the toilet or something, but then it ran off.'
jokes.setup: Leslie demands to know how the possum got loose in Ann's house
jokes.punchline: April's logic — release a captured possum to let it find its own water, specifically anticipating it would use the toilet
jokes.explanation: The possum-toilet logic is absurd but delivered with April's characteristic straight-faced certainty. The specific detail of thinking it would use the toilet is funny — it shows April's complete lack of knowledge about wildlife combined with her typical don't-care attitude.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, I think this is great news. We can finally tell the difference between ducks and geese.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, do you understand what you're saying? We have been lying to the people of Pawnee. Every time someone asked us about the waterfowl in that pond, we lied. We looked them in the eye and we lied.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not just a mistake, Tom. That's a betrayal of the public trust.

jokes.text: April: 'It must love tacky pictures of flowers.' — looking at Ann's décor while searching for the possum
jokes.setup: The possum has apparently moved to a room with flower pictures on the wall
jokes.punchline: April takes a moment in the middle of the possum crisis to insult Ann's taste in home décor
jokes.explanation: April's inability to stop herself from criticizing Ann even during a genuine emergency is perfect character comedy. The timing — mid-crisis — and the casual delivery make it funnier. Classic April.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, April just called me. She needs help with something, but she made me promise not to tell you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Tom, you have to tell me!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know, I know. But I promised.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. She said—

jokes.text: Mark shows up at Ron's shop with tools: 'I haven't even started yet.' 'I know. Thought you could use some help.'
jokes.setup: Ron faces his woodshop code violations with 24 hours to fix them.
jokes.punchline: Mark shows up uninvited to help, knowing Ron won't do it himself. 'Those city planning guys can be real pains in the ass.' Ron agrees — about Mark specifically, who is standing in front of him.
jokes.explanation: A warm friendship moment with a mild joke — Ron agreeing that 'city planning guys' are pains in the ass when talking to Mark, the city planner who is there to help him, is gently ironic. Works more as a character beat than a straight joke.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, it makes sense that a possum would feel at home here. This place looks like a dead animal's nest.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'No, I am bringing my workshop up to the Swanson Code. And if the Swanson Code happens to overlap with the City Government Code...' — Mark cuts him off: 'Shut up.'
jokes.setup: Ron wants to frame his compliance with code as compliance with the 'Swanson Code' — his own invented standard
jokes.punchline: Mark cuts him off before he can finish the rationalization
jokes.explanation: A good running gag payoff — Ron rebranding city code compliance as 'the Swanson Code' to maintain his dignity. Mark's preemptive shutdown is the right button. The running-gag structure is well-maintained throughout the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey Ron, I know we don't always see eye to eye, but I'm here to help if you need it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't need your help, Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Ron, shut up. But like, in a friendly way.

jokes.text: Leslie worries the possum has 'laid eggs in the bed.' April: 'What if it's in here? What if it laid eggs in the bed?'
jokes.setup: Leslie and April are searching Ann's house for the escaped possum.
jokes.punchline: Leslie raises the factually wrong fear that the possum laid eggs in the bed — possums are marsupials, not egg-layers. The terror is based on false biology.
jokes.explanation: A mild absurdist joke — possums don't lay eggs, but Leslie and April don't know that. The fear is funny because it's based on animal ignorance. Works as a mild cringe-comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, the system works if you let it work.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Shut up.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're not listening to my point about—

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Shut up.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But the key thing is—

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Shut up.

jokes.text: April confesses she doesn't want to call Andy because 'it's my fault it's in Ann's house, who he's obviously still in love with. I just don't want him to be mad at me.'
jokes.setup: April needs to call Andy for possum help but is resistant
jokes.punchline: The reason for reluctance — April's feelings for Andy are exposed; she's worried about his reaction and what he thinks of her in relation to Ann
jokes.explanation: This is more character development than pure comedy, but it's warm and funny in its indirectness. April revealing her feelings through logistical concern is very April. The cringe/warmth balance is typical of Parks' best character moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, so possums don't actually play dead to avoid predators? They just... collapse from fear?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's correct.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So if I threaten a possum, it will just faint?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's the dumbest animal I've ever heard of. What evolutionary advantage is that?

jokes.text: Leslie says 'And, April, any time you want to talk about boys...' — April: 'Oh, my God! Stop!'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just witnessed April's vulnerability about Andy; she tries to offer herself as a mentor/confidante
jokes.punchline: April's horrified response — 'Oh, my God! Stop!' — perfectly conveys her absolute unwillingness to be in a feelings conversation with Leslie
jokes.explanation: April's reaction is the entire joke — the visceral disgust at being offered emotional support from Leslie. It's also funny because Leslie was trying to be sweet. Good character-pair dynamic comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am not calling Andy. He's just going to come over here and try to fix everything, and be all charming and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That sounds terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It is! And then Ann will see how great he is, and she'll fall for him, and I'll be stuck watching the two of them together.

jokes.text: Andy arrives with a list of everything he did that might have upset Tom, and also coffee, to apologize
jokes.setup: Andy senses Tom is mad at him but doesn't know why
jokes.punchline: Andy's solution: compile a comprehensive list of everything he did, present it with coffee, and promise not to do any of them again
jokes.explanation: The list approach is very Andy — thorough in the wrong direction, earnest, slightly confused. The 'I'm gonna try not to do any of them again' is a good line implying the list is probably quite long and/or disturbing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He's not mad at you. Andy doesn't get mad. He gets excited about things and then forgets about them.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not reassuring.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but it's true.

jokes.text: Andy reads the newspaper article where he credited April for 'liquid courage' for tackling the possum — crediting April's coffee as essential to his heroism
jokes.setup: Andy shows April the published article as evidence of his gratitude
jokes.punchline: The article credits coffee from April as essential 'liquid courage' to wrestle the possum — a wildly disproportionate credit that reveals Andy's character
jokes.explanation: Andy formally crediting coffee as 'liquid courage for possum wrestling' in a published newspaper article is both sweet and absurd. It also ties back to the shoeshine head coffee cure established early in the episode, giving it a callback quality. Good warm comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I want you to know that I'm here for you. If you ever need to talk about your feelings, or just have a girls' night in, I'm your person.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Leslie, no. Absolutely not. I would rather eat a bowl of nails than sit around talking about feelings with you or anyone else.

jokes.text: Andy made a list of everything he did to upset April and plans not to do any of them again — and also brought coffee.
jokes.setup: Andy approaches April, worried he upset her the previous day.
jokes.punchline: He's made a formal list of all his offenses — thoughtful, considerate Andy behavior — but leads with the tangible gift (coffee), which undercuts the earnestness charmingly.
jokes.explanation: A sweet Andy moment that works as mild comedy — the formal list of offenses is both touching and funny. The coffee as simultaneous olive branch is classic Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm giving April credit in the newspaper for helping me with this article.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Thanks, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I needed some liquid courage just to get through writing it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You drank coffee?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A lot of coffee. Also, I called that possum a beast. Did you see that?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, that possum was a beast.

jokes.text: Andy's article quote: he gives credit to April for 'the liquid courage I needed to wrestle that beast to the ground.'
jokes.setup: Andy shows April the newspaper article where he was quoted.
jokes.punchline: He credits April's coffee as the 'liquid courage' he needed — treating coffee as if it were courage-inducing alcohol, making his possum tackle sound like a military operation requiring Dutch courage.
jokes.explanation: Calling coffee 'liquid courage' is a nice Andy-ism — it treats possum-tackling with the gravity of war heroism. The gesture itself (giving April credit in print) is the warm part, and the inflated language is the funny part.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to be remembered as a visionary leader who transformed this town. Libraries will be named after me. Streets will bear my name. And when historians look back at my greatest accomplishment, they'll focus on one thing: the blue hat I wore to the gala.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to Leslie's resolution of the possum situation: 'Well, Miss Knope. I have to say I'm very disappointed.' — Leslie: 'You didn't have to say that, you could've just thought it.'
jokes.setup: Ron learns that Leslie released the possum rather than having it killed
jokes.punchline: Ron expresses disappointment; Leslie immediately tells him he could have kept it to himself
jokes.explanation: Leslie's response — 'you could've just thought it' — is a good quick retort. It's a small moment but economical and lands the beat cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, there was a small fire. Then a medium fire. Then a very large fire.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head on her future: she imagines attending a gala 'honoring the first three female presidents in history, myself and two other women I've inspired' while 'wearing a huge, beautiful, blue hat'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains why she released the possum — she doesn't want her legacy to be possum-related
jokes.punchline: Her vision of the future is aspirational but the specific blue hat detail makes it absurd and deeply personal
jokes.explanation: This joke works on multiple levels. Leslie envisions herself as one of three future female presidents (pure Leslie ambition), but the emotional core of the joke is 'a huge, beautiful, blue hat.' The hat is the detail that makes it both funny and oddly moving — she's imagined this future so precisely she knows what she'll be wearing. It's character comedy at the highest level of Parks and Recreation. Justifies 8+ through its specificity and perfect Leslie-ness.

jokes.text: April's parting words while fleeing: 'Sorry, Ann! I love you!'
jokes.setup: April is running away from Ann after the possum disaster
jokes.punchline: April — who flatly stated 'I don't like Ann' at the top of the episode — shouts 'I love you!' while literally running away from the consequences of her actions
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect callback. The episode opens with April's flat 'I don't like Ann' intercut with Ann's hopes for friendship. The episode closes with April — in full flight from Ann's house, having caused chaos — shouting 'I love you!' while running away. The callback structure is beautiful: the same relationship, exactly inverted, under absurd circumstances. It's also genuinely earned because we've seen April's vulnerability about wanting Andy to like her, suggesting she IS capable of caring. Three words close the episode perfectly. This is one of the best jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have to go!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I love you, Ann!

jokes.text: Ann's final reaction: 'I'm gonna go. / I think that would be best.'
jokes.setup: Ann has just been informed her house was invaded by a possum that touched all her bras, and April has fled
jokes.punchline: Ann's response to the chaos is a flat, dignified 'I'm gonna go' — the understatement of the situation
jokes.explanation: Good button on the final scene. Ann's dignified retreat from the situation — choosing to leave rather than process any of this — and Leslie's 'I think that would be best' is a clean, quiet closer. The understatement works.

tmdb_overview: When a possum bites the mayor's dog on a golf course, Leslie is asked to form a task force to catch the pesky animal. Meanwhile, Ron is upset when Mark refuses to bend the rules for him.
insight: Absurdist escalation hits 77 jokes in 23 minutes, but impact stays below Parks' season average.
